newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - BICC cash gains boost optimism.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - BICC cash gains boost optimism.

text.p: The chief executive of British cable manufacturer and civil engineering group BICC Plc said on Wednesday that an encouragingly strong cash performance in 1996 underpinned his optimism for growth from ongoing investments in 1997 and beyond.

Speaking after BICC reported 1996 pretax profits of 129 million stg before exceptional items, Alan Jones told Reuters that the company's year-end net debt of 80 million stg was "about half what the city expected".

These gains, coupled with the resources provided by a 170 million stg rights issue last year, meant the group was poised to increase capital expenditure by about 40 percent in 1997 for the second year running.
In a telephone interview Jones described the ongoing reorganisation and redirection of capital as "a reinvestment phase".

Across cables and construction BICC has consolidated its existing businesses and sought to reduce exposure and tied-up capital in low margin sectors -- improving cash performance and creating more room for a big push into data and communications cables.

No further major closures or reductions were expected in traditional cables in Europe, Jones said, adding that Balfour Beatty had pulled out of general construction in the United States but was retaining a healthy heavy civil engineering business there.
He saw an improving outlook for Balfour Beatty, explaining that "we said at the half year that we were likely to see only limited profit performance improvement in the short term."
"We are now seeing benefits from the actions taken which should gradually improve performance," he added.

Balfour Beatty's latest expansion into rail maintenance and track renewal, supported by the acquisition of three ex-British Rail units during last year's privatisation, has enhanced the group's technology base but is not expected to bring near-term profitability gains in the UK.

"It's a good strong business, but we've got some rationalisation to do," Jones said, adding that the group's international business expected to reap wider benefits from these units' expertise in future.
